implementation_notes: scala.util.Using is the standard library's realization: Using.resource opens, runs the body and releases even when the body throws (behaving like Java's try-with-resources and throwing the body's exception), Using.apply wraps the whole operation in Try, and Using.Manager releases an arbitrary number of resources registered during the body in reverse acquisition order. What replaces the classic wrapper is that object plus the implicit Releasable instance for AutoCloseable - supply your own Releasable when release is not a close() method. Use it for any Closeable resource and prefer it over a hand-written loan method so failure handling and suppression are the standard library's problem.
pitfalls: Using.apply returns Try[A]: ignoring that result silently swallows a failure, so unwrap it or pattern-match explicitly.

Using.resource rejects a null resource with NullPointerException instead of skipping it, and a release failure is suppressed onto the body's exception according to a scoring rule that is easy to overlook in logs.
A by-name resource argument is evaluated when the body runs, so an acquisition with side effects must be a stable expression; otherwise retries or re-entry acquire twice.

variants.name: loan pattern with a by-name body parameter
variants.idiom_name: def withConnection[R](url: String)(body: Connection => R): R
variants.implementation_notes: For protocols the standard library does not model, Scala's idiom is the loan pattern: a method acquires the resource, calls the body with it, and releases in a finally block; the body is a function value, so the call site reads as a block and the result type is inferred. By-name and function-typed parameters make this a two-line method, which is why it predates Using and still suits domain protocols (unit of work, retry bracket, tenant context) where the release logic is specific. Use Using for plain Closeable resources so suppression behaviour is standardized, and the loan method when the resource type or release protocol is your own.
pitfalls: A finally that throws replaces the body's exception; log or suppress the release failure deliberately instead of letting it win by default.
A by-name parameter is re-evaluated at every reference, so a wrapper that mentions it twice runs the body twice - bind it to a val first.
The loan method cannot prevent the body from leaking the resource (returning it, storing it in a field): the convention is the guarantee, not the compiler.
